Weight is mass times directional force. This is usually gravity, but can also be (for example) the centripetal force in a rotating reference frame. Gravity in low Earth orbit is only attenuated by approximately 0.8m/s. If you were to stop the station in mid-flight you would experience nearly the same amount of gravity as on Earth's surface. The station has weight from any reference frame smaller than the Sun's. It's only things inside the freefalling station's reference frame that experience weightlessness, i.e. one object (e.g. astronaut) moving another (e.g. 275lb space suit) requires only enough force exerted on the reference body, the station, to overcome momentum. If your reference frame were the Sun and you could physically push off of Earth in this manner you'd see the same effect, because the Earth has the weight in that reference frame.

The station in low Earth orbit weighs approximately 8.6 tons. More at re-entry. It's only when you include Earth's orbiting body (and use a simplified non n-body gravity calculation) in your model that it is in any way weightless at that altitude.
